claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element automotive alloy containing several principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios.
Post-synthesis thermal or plasma-assisted exposure to an NH3-containing atmosphere can incorporate nitrogen into the catalyst's near-surface region.
Nitridation will produce robust metal–nitrogen bonds at the catalyst surface.
Controlled nitridation can be performed without disturbing the catalyst's bulk phase.
The treatment will form a thin, nitride-rich surface layer containing well-dispersed metal–nitrogen bonds.
Metal–nitrogen bonding stabilizes catalytically active sites.
The nitride-rich layer inhibits active-metal migration and aggregation or sintering.
The nitride-rich layer inhibits active-metal leaching.
Metal–nitrogen bonding stabilizes the catalyst surface against chemical attack by H2O and NO.
Metal–nitrogen bonding stabilizes the catalyst surface against thermal fluctuations and thermal aging.
Nitridation will improve catalytic activity retention relative to the untreated catalyst during transient, low-temperature automotive exhaust operation.
Nitridation will improve durability relative to the untreated catalyst under H2O and NO exposure and accelerated thermal aging.
The improvement can be achieved without increasing platinum-group-metal content.
Nitrogen doping and multiple metal–nitrogen bonds can enhance activity, corrosion resistance, and durability in a Pt-containing high-entropy alloy electrocatalyst.
The magnitude of improvement under complex automotive exhaust conditions may depend sensitively on nitridation conditions and catalyst microstructure.
